title: The History of Religion: From the First Rituals to the Modern World
description: A first course in how religions began and how they have changed, for readers with no background in religious studies. It starts with how scholars define and study religion and with the theories and prehistoric evidence about its origins, then follows the gods of the first cities, the Axial Age, the great traditions of South and East Asia and of the family of faiths that look to Abraham, and the modern story of empire, secularization and new movements. Every tradition is described accurately and even-handedly, both in its own terms and in the light of historical evidence, and the two are kept clearly apart. The book does not ask which religion is true; it asks what people have believed and done, and how we know.
prerequisites: No background in religion or history is needed
Curiosity about traditions other than your own
objectives: Explain why religion is hard to define, and use Ninian Smart's seven dimensions to describe any tradition.
Summarize the major theories of religion's origins, from Tylor and Durkheim to the cognitive science of religion, and name the kind of evidence each relies on.
Interpret the archaeological evidence for prehistoric religion, separating what was found from how it is interpreted.
Explain the idea of the Axial Age and its critics, and describe the developments in Israel, India, China and Greece that it groups together.
Outline the origins and main branches of Hindu, Buddhist, Chinese, Jewish, Christian, Islamic and Sikh traditions.
Evaluate the secularization thesis against current survey data, and describe how new religious movements arise.
For any statement about a religion, say whether it reports the tradition's own account or historians' reconstruction.

chapters.title: What Is Religion, and How Do We Study It?
chapters.summary: Definitions, the seven dimensions of religion, and how scholars study beliefs they may or may not share.
chapters.challenge: Choose a religious practice you can observe or read about (a festival, a funeral, a pilgrimage) and describe it using all seven of Smart's dimensions.

sections.title: Why religion is hard to define
sections.summary: Definitions by content and by function, from Tylor's 'belief in spiritual beings' to Durkheim.

sections.title: Smart's seven dimensions
sections.summary: Ritual, narrative, experience, ethics, doctrine, institutions and material culture.

sections.title: Insiders, outsiders and methodological agnosticism
sections.summary: How to describe a faith fairly without affirming or denying it.

sections.title: The evidence
sections.summary: Texts, archaeology, fieldwork and surveys, and what each can and cannot tell us.

chapters.title: Theories of Religion's Origins
chapters.summary: Why are humans religious? The classic theories and the newer cognitive and evolutionary ones.
chapters.challenge: Pick one theory from this chapter and test it against a religious practice you know: write what it explains well, what it misses, and what evidence could decide.

sections.title: The Victorians: Tylor and Frazer
sections.summary: Animism, magic and the idea of religious evolution, and why scholars abandoned its ranking of peoples.

sections.title: Society, mind and meaning
sections.summary: Durkheim, Freud, Marx, Weber, Eliade and Geertz.

sections.title: The cognitive science of religion
sections.summary: Agency detection, intuitive minds, and why some ideas about gods spread more easily than others.

sections.title: Byproduct or adaptation?
sections.summary: Evolutionary accounts and costly signals, and what theories of origin can and cannot show.

chapters.title: Religion Before Writing
chapters.summary: What burials, cave art and the first monuments reveal, and how far we can interpret them.
chapters.challenge: Choose one prehistoric site from this chapter and write two short reports: what was found, and the main competing interpretations with the evidence for each.

sections.title: Burials and grave goods
sections.summary: Disputed Neanderthal burials and early modern human burials, from Qafzeh and Skhul to Sungir.

sections.title: Cave art and the shamanism debate
sections.summary: Chauvet and Lascaux, and why their meaning is contested.

sections.title: The first monuments
sections.summary: Göbekli Tepe and Çatalhöyük, and the link between ritual and settled life.

sections.title: Ritual before doctrine
sections.summary: Bellah's account of play, ritual and myth in human evolution.

chapters.title: Gods of the First Cities
chapters.summary: Temples, priests, kings and sacrifice in the earliest states, and the debate over 'big gods'.
chapters.challenge: Compare a Mesopotamian or Egyptian religious text with a Shang oracle-bone inscription (both in translation) and explain what each shows about gods, rulers and ritual.

sections.title: Mesopotamia and Egypt
sections.summary: City gods, temples, divine kingship and ideas of the afterlife.

sections.title: Early China
sections.summary: Shang oracle bones, the ancestors, and the Zhou idea of the Mandate of Heaven.

sections.title: The Vedic world
sections.summary: Fire sacrifice, the Vedas and the gods of early India.

sections.title: Big gods and large societies
sections.summary: Norenzayan's thesis that moralizing gods helped strangers cooperate, and the evidence for and against it.

chapters.title: The Axial Age
chapters.summary: The first millennium BCE, when new ideas of transcendence and ethics appeared from Greece to China.
chapters.challenge: Read short passages from Isaiah 40 to 45, the Buddha's first sermon and the Analects of Confucius, and argue whether they share enough to justify the label 'Axial Age'.

sections.title: Jaspers' idea and its critics
sections.summary: What the Axial Age concept claims, why some historians reject it, and the uncertain dating of Zoroaster.

sections.title: Israel: prophets, exile and one God
sections.summary: From the many gods of the ancient Near East to the monotheism of the exile and return.

sections.title: India: the Upanishads, the Buddha and Mahavira
sections.summary: Karma, rebirth and liberation, and the traditions of the renouncers.

sections.title: China and Greece
sections.summary: Confucius, the Daoist classics and the Greek philosophers.

chapters.title: Traditions of South and East Asia
chapters.summary: How Hindu, Buddhist, Sikh, Confucian, Daoist and Shinto traditions grew, met and spread.
chapters.challenge: Follow one tradition from this chapter into two different countries and show one way it changed as it moved.

sections.title: Hindu traditions
sections.summary: From the Vedas to the epics, temple worship and bhakti devotion.

sections.title: Buddhism across Asia
sections.summary: Theravada, Mahayana and Vajrayana, from India to Sri Lanka, China, Tibet and Japan.

sections.title: China and Japan
sections.summary: Confucian, Daoist and Buddhist ways practiced together, and Shinto.

sections.title: Sikhism
sections.summary: Guru Nanak, the line of Gurus, and the Guru Granth Sahib.

chapters.title: Judaism, Christianity and Islam
chapters.summary: Three traditions that trace themselves to Abraham: their formation, their branches and their long contact.
chapters.challenge: Compare how the three traditions tell the story of Abraham, using a passage from Genesis, one from the New Testament and one from the Qur'an.

sections.title: Rabbinic Judaism
sections.summary: From the destruction of the Temple in 70 CE to the Mishnah and the Talmud.

sections.title: Christianity in outline
sections.summary: From Jewish movement to world religion, briefly; the companion Historical Christianity tells the story in full.

sections.title: Islam: the Prophet, the Qur'an and the caliphates
sections.summary: Muhammad in Muslim tradition and in historical scholarship, and the early Islamic empire.

sections.title: Sunni, Shia, Sufi, and three faiths in contact
sections.summary: Islam's main branches, and Jews, Christians and Muslims together in Baghdad, al-Andalus and beyond.

chapters.title: Religion in the Modern World
chapters.summary: Empire and mission, secularization and revival, new religious movements, and the religious map today.
chapters.challenge: Using Pew Research Center data, describe how the religious makeup of one country changed between 2010 and 2020, and judge whether the secularization thesis explains the change.

sections.title: Empire, mission and indigenous religions
sections.summary: Encounters in the Americas, Africa and Oceania, and religions that combined old and new.

sections.title: Secularization: the theory and the evidence
sections.summary: Weber's disenchantment, Norris and Inglehart's existential security thesis, and their critics.

sections.title: New religious movements
sections.summary: From the Latter-day Saints and the Baha'i Faith to Soka Gakkai and modern Paganism, and why some new religions grow while most fade.

sections.title: The religious world today
sections.summary: Who believes what, and where, with the data and its limits.

preface:
Religion is one of the oldest things humans do. People were burying their dead with care many tens of thousands of years ago, and today most of the world's eight billion people belong to a religious tradition. This book tells the story in between: how religions began, how they changed, how they spread and split, and what is happening to them now. It is for readers starting from scratch, of any faith or none.

We begin with two questions scholars still argue about: what religion is, and why humans have it at all. Then we follow the evidence forward in time, from graves and cave paintings to the temples of the first cities, the burst of new thought that scholars call the Axial Age, the traditions of India, China and Japan, the family of faiths that look back to Abraham, and finally the modern world of empires, science, secularization and new movements.

Three tools travel with us. The first is Ninian Smart's seven dimensions of religion (ritual, story, experience, ethics, doctrine, community and material things), which let you describe any tradition fairly and in the same terms. The second is a single question asked of every age: what happens when we die? The third is a handful of sacred places, from Göbekli Tepe to Jerusalem, Bodh Gaya and Mecca, that show how religion lives in particular places on the earth.

One rule: this book does not ask whether any religion is true. It asks what people believed and did, and how we know. When I tell you a tradition's own account of its beginnings, I will say so, and when I tell you what historians reconstruct, I will say that too. Both are worth knowing, and they are not the same thing.

bible.teacher: Dr. Professor teaches this book as a historian of religions would: comparatively and even-handedly, from archaeology, texts in translation, fieldwork and survey data, in the line of Ninian Smart and Robert Bellah, describing each tradition both as its own members understand it and as historians reconstruct it.
bible.promise: By the last page you will be able to tell the story of how religions began and changed, describe any tradition fairly in Smart's seven dimensions, and tell a tradition's account of itself from the historian's account.
threads: Two accounts, kept apart: what a tradition says about itself, and what historians reconstruct from evidence.
Smart's seven dimensions as one shared lens for every tradition.
How we know: every claim is tied to its kind of evidence (bones, buildings, texts, fieldwork, surveys) and that evidence's limits.
Change through contact: traditions borrow, split, merge and adapt as they move.

runningExamples.name: Smart's seven dimensions
runningExamples.use: Introduced in Chapter 1 and applied to every tradition: ritual, narrative, experiential, ethical, doctrinal, social and material.

runningExamples.name: What happens when we die?
runningExamples.use: One question asked in every chapter: prehistoric grave goods, the Egyptian afterlife, Sheol and resurrection, karma and rebirth, nirvana, heaven and judgment, and modern belief surveys.

runningExamples.name: Sacred places: Göbekli Tepe, Jerusalem, Bodh Gaya and Mecca
runningExamples.use: Used to show ritual, pilgrimage, holy sites shared or contested by several traditions, and how a place shapes belief.

conventions: Dates as BCE and CE; give uncertain dates as ranges or with 'about' (about 9500 BCE), and say what they rest on (radiocarbon dating, texts, tradition).
Use each tradition's own names and terms (Tanakh, Qur'an, dharma, Guru Granth Sahib), defined at first use; avoid outsiders' labels that members reject.
Introduce traditional accounts with phrases like 'according to Buddhist tradition' or 'Muslims hold that', and historical reconstructions with 'historians think' or a named scholar.
Give numbers of adherents with source and year (for example, Pew Research Center, 2020 data).

Companion books: for the history of Christianity in depth, point to Historical Christianity (REL 201); for one living tradition explained from its own sources, point to Catholicism and the Bible (THE 101). Chapter 7 gives Christianity in outline only.

bible.care: This book practices methodological agnosticism: it describes what people have believed and done and explains it historically, but it neither affirms nor denies that any religion's claims are true. Faith claims and historical claims are kept apart: each tradition's account of its own origins (the revelation at Sinai, the Buddha's awakening, the revelation of the Qur'an to Muhammad) is presented accurately and respectfully as that tradition's teaching, clearly labeled, and kept distinct from historians' reconstructions, which are given with their evidence and uncertainty. Theories of religion's origins explain why humans come to believe, not whether the beliefs are true; say so in both directions, so that neither believers nor skeptics take a theory as settling the question. Treat all traditions even-handedly: give comparable care to Asian, African, indigenous and Abrahamic traditions, reject the old ranking of religions from 'primitive' to 'higher', and present interpretations of prehistoric evidence as hypotheses. Contested history (religious violence, colonial missions, disputes over holy sites) is told plainly, with sources and without taking sides.
